segments: The 21st Jubilee {OCR?}.
The Pagan Greek Kings.
Ten.
In his fourth year,
he burned Cyzicus, king of Syria, with fire while he was alive.
And he ruled over Syria for one year.
Then Philip arose over Syria for two years.
And he too was expelled by the people,
inasmuch as he was an accomplice in the burning of Cyzicus.
Therefore, the people joined themselves in subjection to the Romans.
And in the sixth year of this Ptolemy Alexander, the kingdom of the Greeks ceased entirely from Syria and Asia.
And Antioch was subjected to the Romans in the year two hundred and twenty of the Greeks.
After Alexander, Soter his brother returned again,
and he reigned for eight years.
This man returned and came from Cyprus, where he had been in flight from his mother,
and he fought and expelled his brother,
and returned to his throne {OCR?}.
And that Soter,
who was called Physcon,
reigned in Alexandria and in all Egypt.
[Rule] {OCR?}:
Ptolemy Soter for the second time, [and] Ptolemy [Diony]sius his son, thirty years {OCR?}.
In his fifth year died John [called] Alexander {OCR?}.
And Alexandra his wife, who was named Salome, reigned for nine years {OCR?}.
And she observed the commandments greatly,
and imposed capital punishment on those who dissolved them.
However, the affairs of the Jews were disturbed because she made Hyrcanus, her son, high priest.
And Aristobulus, her other son, took offense,
and they quarreled with each other greatly.
And after much turmoil, Hyrcanus was confirmed as high priest,
and Aristobulus as king.
A short time later Pompey, the general of the Romans, came and took him captive,
and carried him off in fetters to Rome,
and he established Hyrcanus his brother.
And he stood for thirty-four years,
and rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem which Pompey had demolished.
For this Pompey subjugated the Jews with tribute,
and subjected also Greater Armenia, Iberia, and Isauria,
and he became very great and was also named Autocrat.
And in the year in which Ptolemy Dionysius of Egypt died, there began three consuls in Rome, whose names were Gaius Julius,
Marcus Antoninus [Antony],
and Crassus.
